paragraphs: Extracting information from a web page involves recognizing how pieces of information fit together. The authors report that information about objects of the same type has strong sequence patterns across different websites. Such patterns make conditional random fields useful: these models can assign labels while taking relationships between neighboring pieces of information into account.

The paper argues that a single sequence does not fully represent the way information appears on a page. Web content is arranged in two dimensions, so relevant neighborhood relationships need not follow one linear chain. The proposed two-dimensional conditional random field incorporates these interactions into the labeling model, making page layout part of the extraction approach.

The authors evaluate the model on product information extraction and compare it with existing linear-chain conditional random fields. Their results support the effectiveness of the two-dimensional model in this setting. The contribution is a way to bring the spatial organization of web information into structured labeling, alongside the sequence regularities that motivated earlier approaches.
icml-2005-2d-conditional-random-fields-f.tldr: A two-dimensional conditional random field uses web-page neighborhood relationships to extract product information effectively.

paragraphs: Different clustering algorithms can produce different groupings of the same data, creating a need to compare their results. This paper develops a distance that considers how far apart cluster representatives are. That makes the locations of the groups part of the comparison, rather than judging the relationship between two clustering results without accounting for those distances.

The proposed measure comes from a complete matching between the clusters in two results, chosen to be globally optimal. The authors show that this construction is an instance of the Mallows distance between probability distributions. This connection supplies mathematical properties for the comparison, including the triangle inequality, which keeps distances among three clustering results mutually consistent.

The framework covers both hard clustering, where membership is definite, and soft clustering, where membership can be distributed across groups. Experiments show that the measure handles cases that are difficult for other comparison methods. Its contribution combines that empirical usefulness with a unified mathematical treatment of different kinds of cluster membership.
icml-2005-a-new-mallows-distance-based-m.tldr: A Mallows-based distance compares hard and soft clusterings through optimal cluster matching while accounting for distances between representatives.

paragraphs: Graph-based semi-supervised learning uses relationships among labeled and unlabeled examples to help classify them. The paper identifies two obstacles to using these methods more broadly. Their inference can require a large matrix inversion or a large linear program, and their predictions are typically restricted to the unlabeled points already included in the problem.

Harmonic mixtures combine a generative mixture model with discriminative regularization based on the graph Laplacian. The mixture model supplies a model-based route to prediction, while the graph component retains information about relationships among examples. This combination is designed to support predictions for arbitrary new test points and reduce the computational burden associated with purely graph-based inference.

The experiments show that the method preserves the accuracy of graph-based transductive approaches when the data has manifold structure. In the same setting, it achieves inductive prediction with significantly lower computational cost. The result supports combining these two modeling approaches when the aim is to retain graph-based learning benefits while extending prediction beyond a fixed collection of unlabeled examples.
icml-2005-harmonic-mixtures-combining-mi.tldr: Harmonic mixtures combine mixture models and graph regularization to predict new examples efficiently while preserving graph-based accuracy on data with manifold structure.

paragraphs: Classification commonly starts with data represented as vectors and then learns boundaries that separate classes. This paper reverses that order. It fixes the decision boundaries and learns where to place the data points relative to them. The representation of the data therefore becomes a central part of the learning problem, rather than a starting point supplied in advance.

The approach requires only pairwise dissimilarities: information about how unlike two examples are. Those dissimilarities do not need to satisfy the stronger requirements of a metric. The learned positions also form a low-dimensional embedding, so the representation can be examined visually. These two features connect classification-oriented learning with data that is initially described through relationships between examples.

The method combines an entropy-based embedding procedure with an entropy-based form of semi-supervised logistic regression. The authors present results for both clustering and semi-supervised classification. The contribution is the alternative formulation itself: learning a useful arrangement of examples around fixed boundaries, while producing a representation that can support visual analysis.
icml-2005-large-margin-non-linear-embedd.tldr: The method learns low-dimensional data positions around fixed decision boundaries using only pairwise dissimilarities.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning when examples are connected by a directed graph and only some examples have labels. A directed connection distinguishes a link from one example to another from a link going the other way. The proposed framework uses both the graph structure and this direction information when learning from labeled and unlabeled data.

The framework also covers the case in which no labels are available. In that setting, it becomes a spectral clustering method for directed graphs, extending the corresponding approach for undirected graphs. This connects classification with partial supervision and clustering without supervision within one framework, while retaining the distinction between the two directions of a relationship.

The algorithm derived from the framework has nearly linear time complexity through the use of numerical techniques. That computational property matters for applying graph-based learning to large collections of linked examples. The authors apply the framework to real-world web classification problems and report encouraging results, providing empirical support for the approach in the application they studied.
icml-2005-learning-from-labeled-and-unla.tldr: A nearly linear-time framework uses directed graph structure for semi-supervised classification and, without labels, spectral clustering.

paragraphs: Preference data often consists of rankings collected through questionnaires, voting forms, or similar inquiries. Clustering these rankings aims to find groups with typical patterns of preference. A complication is that people may fill in different numbers of rank positions, so the observations do not all have the same length.

The paper introduces a mixture model that describes and compares rankings of different lengths within a single probabilistic framework. It uses a maximum entropy approach to avoid introducing hidden assumptions about the unfilled positions. This allows incomplete rankings to participate in the analysis while respecting the distinction between observed preferences and information that was never provided.

The authors derive parameter estimators and an efficient expectation-maximization algorithm for learning the ranking mixture without supervision. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show significantly better parameter estimates when incomplete rankings are included in inference on heterogeneous data. The finding supports retaining partial responses as useful evidence for identifying preference groups through the proposed model.
icml-2007-cluster-analysis-of-heterogene.tldr: A maximum-entropy mixture model clusters rankings of different lengths and improves parameter estimates by incorporating incomplete responses.

paragraphs: A support vector machine can base its prediction rule on only a subset of the training examples while still using every input feature. This paper targets feature sparsity: a decision rule with fewer nonzero feature weights. It starts from a formulation that explicitly limits how many weights can be nonzero, creating a nonconvex optimization problem.

The authors propose two convex relaxations of that formulation. One produces a quadratically constrained quadratic program and can be understood as adaptively soft-thresholding the weights of the separating hyperplane. The other uses semidefinite programming to learn a weighted inner product, or kernel, that yields a sparse hyperplane. Both formulations address the feature-count constraint through a convex optimization route.

Experiments compare the methods with a standard SVM and a linear programming SVM. The reported results show greater sparsity while preserving generalization performance in those comparisons. The contribution is therefore a pair of optimization formulations that seek more selective feature use, with empirical evidence that this selectivity need not reduce predictive performance in the tested settings.
icml-2007-direct-convex-relaxations-of-s.tldr: Two convex relaxations produce SVMs with fewer active features while preserving generalization performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: A classification system may be trained on examples whose distribution differs from that of the examples it will later encounter. This paper addresses that situation under the heading of covariate shift. Within the stated setting, the distribution governing training instances is allowed to differ arbitrarily from the test distribution, making that mismatch part of the learning problem.

The proposed solution is purely discriminative: it learns a classifier without explicitly modeling either the training distribution or the test distribution. The authors formulate learning under covariate shift as an integrated optimization problem. This gives the distribution mismatch a place within the classifier's optimization rather than requiring explicit probability models of the two instance populations.

From that formulation, the paper derives a kernel logistic regression classifier for differing training and test distributions. Its stated contribution is a mathematical and algorithmic route to classification under covariate shift. The approach matters because it connects this mismatch problem with discriminative classifier training while avoiding the separate task of explicitly modeling both distributions.
icml-2007-discriminative-learning-for-di.tldr: The paper derives a kernel logistic regression approach to covariate shift without explicitly modeling training or test distributions.

paragraphs: A confidence region identifies parameter values compatible with observed data while controlling the probability of incorrectly excluding the true value. Smaller expected regions offer greater precision, but finding procedures with this property can be computationally difficult for complex models. This paper focuses on making the Minimax Expected-Size confidence procedure more practical to compute.

The central calculation in that procedure is an equilibrium of a particular zero-sum game. The authors show that the game is convex and has bilinear payoffs, opening it to convex game solvers, including linear programming. This characterization connects the statistical objective to optimization methods that can be used to carry out the required computation.

The implementation exploits sparsity in the game's matrix and uses fast linear programming software. Together, these choices allow approximate minimax expected-size confidence regions to be computed orders of magnitude faster than previously published methods. The authors test the approaches by estimating parameters of a cosmological model. The reported advance concerns the computational accessibility of the confidence-region procedure, with the regions explicitly described as approximate.
icml-2007-efficiently-computing-minimax-.tldr: A convex-game formulation and sparse linear programming compute approximate minimax expected-size confidence regions orders of magnitude faster.

paragraphs: Feature selection seeks information that is useful for distinguishing classes and analyzing data. This paper considers selection inside a kernel space, whose dimension may be infinite. That makes the problem different from choosing among a finite list of measured input variables: the space in which selection occurs first needs a usable representation.

The authors begin by deriving a basis set in the kernel space. They then use that basis to extend margin-based feature selection algorithms that are effective even when many features depend on one another. The selected features define a subspace of the kernel space, providing a reduced representation in which classification can take place.

Different classification algorithms can operate within the resulting subspace, so the selection procedure is not tied to a single final classifier. The authors evaluate their method on real and simulated data against four baseline algorithms. Both their theoretical analysis and experimental results support its effectiveness. The contribution brings feature selection into the kernel representation itself and supplies a route for using the selected information in subsequent classification.
icml-2007-feature-selection-in-a-kernel-.tldr: The method constructs a kernel-space basis and selects useful features to form a subspace for classification.

paragraphs: Focused crawling aims to discover web resources relevant to a particular interest. This paper treats that task as a large-scale ordinal regression problem, which uses ordered outcomes. The formulation avoids requiring a negative class or a topic hierarchy, two requirements the authors identify as major drawbacks of existing focused crawling methods.

To support this application, the paper introduces a scalable ordinal regression formulation based on clustering. It is a second-order cone program with one second-order cone constraint. The authors develop a dedicated algorithm, CB-OR, that solves the formulation more efficiently than general-purpose solvers. The modeling contribution and the computational contribution work together to make the large-scale crawling formulation usable.

Experiments on large synthetic and benchmark datasets demonstrate the solver's scalability. Separate crawling experiments show that the proposed crawler outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in the reported evaluation. These findings support both parts of the contribution: an efficient method for solving the ordinal regression problem and an application that uses it to discover relevant web resources.
icml-2007-focused-crawling-with-scalable.tldr: CB-OR efficiently solves a clustering-based ordinal regression formulation and supports a focused crawler that performs strongly in experiments.

paragraphs: The paper learns similarity from pairs of points known to be similar. Its central idea is to measure how much coding length is saved by encoding a pair jointly instead of encoding its members independently. Similarity is therefore expressed through shared information: a pair receives its relationship score from the benefit of describing the two points together.

Under simple Gaussian assumptions, this construction yields a non-Mahalanobis similarity function that is simple and efficient to learn. The authors also interpret it as a likelihood ratio test and show that the optimal projection preserving the similarity is a variant of Fisher Linear Discriminant. These connections give several mathematical views of the same learned relationship.

Under certain naturally occurring sampling conditions for the similar pairs, the function converges to the known RCA Mahalanobis distance. This is a conditional relationship, rather than an equivalence in every setting. Experiments across many datasets show better performance than alternative Mahalanobis distances learned from the same data, with demonstrations in image retrieval and graph-based clustering.
icml-2007-learning-distance-function-by-.tldr: The method learns similarity from the coding savings of jointly describing similar pairs, yielding strong retrieval and clustering results.

paragraphs: Graph nodes can be ranked through two different perspectives. Laplacian-based methods encourage connected nodes to receive locally smooth scores, while PageRank-style methods use Markov random walks. The paper addresses the relationship between these perspectives for directed graphs, where a simple correspondence was not known, and the lack of generalization guarantees for recent scalable PageRank-learning algorithms.

The authors establish some correspondence results between Laplacian and PageRank approaches and provide new generalization guarantees for the latter. They also extend methods for learning PageRank transition probabilities by introducing an additive margin. This brings another learning component into an approach that determines rankings through the movement probabilities of a random walk.

A further contribution is a general framework for learning scores in a rank-sensitive way, which the authors apply to Laplacian smoothing. The experiments are described as promising. Taken together, the work links theoretical understanding with algorithm design: it clarifies parts of the relationship between graph-ranking approaches and develops learning methods that attend directly to ranking.
icml-2007-learning-random-walks-to-rank-.tldr: The paper connects PageRank learning with Laplacian ranking, adds generalization guarantees, and develops margin-based and rank-sensitive learning methods.

paragraphs: This paper treats color prediction as a tool for lossy compression. It learns a model from the colors of a few representative pixels and uses that model to predict colors elsewhere. The stored representation contains the grayscale image and the representative pixels, supplying the information used to reconstruct a color version of the image.

The colorization component uses graph-based inductive semi-supervised learning. A simple active learning strategy chooses the representative pixels that provide color information. These components address the intensive human involvement required by existing colorization approaches, making the selection of color examples and the prediction of remaining colors part of the proposed compression scheme.

For video, a single model can predict color across many consecutive frames, leading to better compression through reuse of that model. Experiments on a wide variety of images and video sequences demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness. Because the scheme is explicitly lossy, reconstruction means recovering a predicted color image or video rather than guaranteeing an exact copy of every original color value.
icml-2007-learning-to-compress-images-an.tldr: The method compresses images and videos by storing grayscale content and selected pixel colors, then learning to reconstruct the remaining colors.

paragraphs: Learning to rank builds a function that orders objects, such as documents returned by a retrieval system. Many approaches train on pairs of objects, learning which member of each pair should come first. This paper argues that training should also reflect the fact that the eventual prediction is an ordered list of objects.

The proposed listwise approach uses lists as training instances. It introduces two probability models, called permutation probability and top-k probability, to construct a loss function for learning from those lists. These probabilistic descriptions provide a way to evaluate ranking predictions at the list level. A neural network supplies the model, and gradient descent is used to train it.

Experiments on information retrieval show that the proposed listwise approach performs better than the pairwise approach in the reported evaluation. The finding supports the paper's argument for aligning the unit of training with the form of the prediction. The contribution includes both that change in perspective and a concrete probabilistic method for putting listwise learning into practice.
icml-2007-learning-to-rank-from-pairwise.tldr: A probabilistic listwise ranking method trains on lists and outperforms a pairwise approach in information-retrieval experiments.

paragraphs: This paper develops a classifier for situations in which only pairwise similarities between samples are available. Instead of requiring a conventional feature description for every sample, it builds a local generative model from those similarities. The goal is to describe the local distribution associated with each class and use those descriptions to make classification decisions.

The class-conditional distributions are estimated through maximum entropy subject to empirical moment constraints. In plain terms, the model is constrained by measured summaries of the data while using a maximum entropy rule to determine the distribution. The resulting exponential distributions are combined with class prior probabilities and misclassification costs to form the local similarity discriminant analysis classifier.

The evaluation compares local SDA with a non-local version, local and ordinary nearest-centroid classifiers, k-nearest neighbors, and the potential support vector machine. Local SDA is competitive with k-nearest neighbors and the computationally demanding potential SVM. The result shows that a local probabilistic treatment of similarity can deliver competitive classification while retaining explicit use of class probabilities and error costs.
icml-2007-local-similarity-discriminant-.tldr: Local SDA classifies from pairwise similarities using local probabilistic models, class priors, and misclassification costs.

paragraphs: Support vector machines can be extended to classification with multiple classes, but handling large datasets remains a computational concern. Core Vector Machines provide a technique for scaling two-class SVMs. This paper brings that technique to multiclass learning, aiming to preserve the predictive behavior of an SVM while reducing the expense of training on large collections of examples.

The proposed Multiclass Core Vector Machine begins by expressing the multiclass SVM as a quadratic programming problem. Its SVM has vector-valued output, providing a formulation for the multiclass task. The authors then solve this optimization problem using the Core Vector Machine technique, connecting the multiclass formulation to an existing route for scalable SVM computation.

Experiments use several large synthetic and real-world datasets. The authors report generalization performance comparable to an SVM at substantially lower computational expense, along with good scaling as dataset size grows. These are empirical findings about the tested problems. They support the proposed formulation as a practical way to extend the computational benefits of Core Vector Machines to multiclass classification.
icml-2007-multiclass-core-vector-machine.tldr: The Multiclass Core Vector Machine extends scalable SVM training to multiple classes with comparable generalization at lower experimental computational cost.

paragraphs: Multiple instance learning works with groups of instances, called bags, whose labels provide information about the instances inside them. A positive bag must contain at least one positive instance. This paper focuses on sparse positive bags, where only a few members are positive, making that small amount of positive evidence central to the learning task.

The proposed approach enforces the requirement that at least one instance in a positive bag be positive more directly than other SVM-based multiple instance methods. Its design therefore concentrates on the constraint linking an individual instance to the bag's label. That focus matters when a positive label is supported by only a small portion of the bag.

Experiments on artificial and real-world data show greater accuracy than state-of-the-art multiple instance learning methods when positive bags are sparse. When they are not sparse, the method remains competitive. The authors also report the best image-region classification performance in their evaluation. These results support the method's particular suitability for sparse positive evidence while showing usefulness beyond that setting.
icml-2007-multiple-instance-learning-for.tldr: A multiple instance learning method more directly enforces positive-bag constraints and improves accuracy when positive instances are scarce.

paragraphs: This paper explores how quantum computation can accelerate clustering algorithms. It uses the term quantization to mean adapting a classical algorithm through quantum mechanics, usually with speed as the objective. The focus is on bringing this idea to unsupervised learning by developing quantum versions of established computational procedures.

The proposed approach uses variations of Grover's quantum algorithm. The authors illustrate it with three procedures: divisive clustering, k-medians, and the construction of a neighborhood graph. These examples span algorithms that directly create clusters and a procedure that builds relationships among data points. Together, they demonstrate how the proposed quantum approach can be applied to several tasks relevant to clustering.

The paper reports a significant speedup over the classical approach. The stated gain concerns computation, rather than a reported improvement in the quality of the resulting clusters. Its contribution is an initial framework for quantizing clustering procedures, supported by concrete versions of the three algorithms and the speed advantage obtained for the proposed approach.
icml-2007-quantum-clustering-algorithms-.tldr: Quantum variants of Grover's algorithm accelerate divisive clustering, k-medians, and neighborhood-graph construction.

paragraphs: Large log-linear models need optimization methods that can handle many parameters. Limited-memory quasi-Newton optimization, particularly L-BFGS, works well with L2 regularization, but L1 regularization introduces a problem: the objective is not differentiable when a parameter is zero. The paper addresses this obstacle while targeting models with millions of parameters.

The proposed Orthant-Wise Limited-memory Quasi-Newton algorithm, OWL-QN, builds on L-BFGS to optimize an L1-regularized log-likelihood efficiently. The authors also prove that OWL-QN converges to a globally optimal parameter vector. This combines a method designed for large parameter spaces with a stated convergence guarantee for the optimization problem.

In parse-reranking experiments, OWL-QN is several orders of magnitude faster than an alternative algorithm. It is also substantially faster than L-BFGS on the analogous L2-regularized problem. These runtime findings come from the reported task and accompany the separate theoretical convergence result. Together, they establish the paper's contribution as both a scalable training algorithm and a mathematically supported way to handle the nondifferentiability introduced by L1 regularization.
icml-2007-scalable-training-of-l1-regula.tldr: OWL-QN efficiently trains L1-regularized log-linear models with millions of parameters and has a global-optimum convergence guarantee.

paragraphs: Large-margin multiclass learning can become costly when outputs are structured and the number of possible classes is exponential. The paper identifies a particular obstacle for full-gradient optimization: even when the eventual solution is sparse, the gradient can be very large and nonsparse. Computing with that gradient therefore need not benefit from the compactness of the solution.

LaRank addresses this difficulty through randomized exploration inspired by the perceptron algorithm. This gives the optimization process an alternative to relying on the full gradient. The method is motivated by the gap between the large collection of possible optimization directions and the sparse solution that learning ultimately seeks.

On simple multiclass problems, the authors show that LaRank is competitive with gradient-based optimizers. They also find that one pass over the training examples produces test error rates nearly as good as those of the final solution. That result concerns predictive performance after an early pass, and supports the practical usefulness of the randomized approach even before optimization reaches its final result.
icml-2007-solving-multiclass-support-vec.tldr: LaRank uses randomized exploration for multiclass SVM optimization and achieves nearly final test performance after one training pass.

paragraphs: Comparing protein structures is useful when proteins have low sequence similarity. This paper develops kernels that compare proteins through structural alignments without using sequence information. The goal is to turn structural resemblance into a similarity representation that can be used for protein structure classification.

At the center of the method is an alignment algorithm that matches substructures of fixed size using spectral graph matching. The authors derive positive semidefinite kernels representing similarity between these substructures, then use them as building blocks for more sophisticated kernels over protein structures. The construction connects local structural matches with a representation suitable for kernel-based classifiers.

The evaluation uses a 40% sequence-nonredundant collection of structures from 15 SCOP superfamilies. When combined with support vector machines, the kernels achieve performance competitive with CE, a state-of-the-art structure comparison program. The finding supports the use of alignment-derived structural similarities for classification in the evaluated collection. The contribution includes both the substructure alignment method and the kernels built from its comparisons.
icml-2007-structural-alignment-based-ker.tldr: Structural alignment kernels classify proteins without sequence information and perform competitively with CE when used with SVMs.

paragraphs: The rendezvous algorithm estimates missing class labels when both labeled and unlabeled examples are available. It represents examples as nodes in a graph and converts pairwise similarities into transition probabilities for a Markov random walk. These probabilities determine how a particle associated with an example moves among the data points.

Labeled points are absorbing states: once a particle reaches one, it stays there. As the number of steps increases, the algorithm considers the probabilities of absorption at the different labeled points. Those probabilities are then used to derive a distribution over the missing label. The method therefore produces probabilistic information about classes through movement across the similarity graph.

The authors derive a computationally efficient implementation and demonstrate it on real and artificial datasets, including numerical comparisons with other methods. The contribution is a concrete connection between graph-based relationships and uncertainty about class labels. Unlabeled examples participate in the graph on which particles move, while labeled examples provide the absorbing destinations that turn those movements into class information.
icml-2007-the-rendezvous-algorithm-multi.tldr: The rendezvous algorithm predicts class distributions from the probabilities that graph-based random walks reach absorbing labeled examples.

paragraphs: This paper uses unlabeled data to learn feature representations for a discriminative classifier. A generative model helps construct those features, connecting information about the data with the later prediction task. The authors examine this strategy through the two-view feature generation model associated with co-training, where the learning setup provides two views of the examples.

Within that framework, they prove that the optimum predictor can be written as a linear combination of a few features constructed from unlabeled data. This result gives a theoretical reason to focus on learning a compact collection of useful features before discriminative training. The authors derive methods from the analysis that use two views but differ substantially from co-training.

Experiments compare the proposed approach with co-training and expectation-maximization under various data generation conditions. The proposed approach is more robust in those tests. The contribution therefore connects a representation result within the two-view model to practical learning methods, with empirical evidence that this use of unlabeled data can be more robust than the compared approaches.
icml-2007-two-view-feature-generation-mo.tldr: A two-view analysis yields features from unlabeled data and learning methods that are more robust than co-training and EM in experiments.

paragraphs: When a classification problem has many classes, the classes may have characteristics in common. This paper proposes learning those shared characteristics at the same time as the predictors for individual classes. Each predictor is expressed in terms of the learned common structure, making shared representation and class prediction parts of one learning problem.

The authors formulate the joint task as a convex optimization problem using trace-norm regularization. The regularization is the mechanism through which the formulation addresses shared structure across class predictors. Learning both components together allows the common characteristics to be determined in connection with the classification task, rather than requiring them to be specified beforehand.

The paper studies gradient-based optimization in both the linear case and a kernelized setting. These two settings extend the proposed formulation across different forms of classifier representation. The stated contribution is a method for jointly discovering common characteristics and learning multiclass predictors, together with an optimization treatment. It provides a concrete mathematical framework for sharing information across a large collection of classes.
icml-2007-uncovering-shared-structures-i.tldr: A convex trace-norm formulation jointly learns shared characteristics and class predictors for multiclass classification.
